prompt: What does Vite do with the types in a `.ts` file when it serves the planner?
hint: Think of why the app kept running while the checker reported errors.

choices.text: Checks them, and refuses to serve a file that has an error
choices.why: That is what the lesson's first wrong picture expects. Vite checks nothing; `vue-tsc` is a separate program.

choices.text: Strips them and runs the JavaScript underneath
choices.why: Right. The code runs exactly as before; the types are for the checker.

choices.text: Turns each interface into a runtime check on the data
choices.why: Only a prop declared by type gets a runtime check, generated by Vue's compiler, and for a `Session` it is just `Object`.

choices.text: Hands the file to `vue-tsc`, which translates it into JavaScript
choices.why: The script runs `vue-tsc --noEmit`, which writes no files at all: it reports and nothing else.

prompt: After renaming every file and changing nothing else, how many errors did `npm run type-check` report?
hint: The transcript that counts lines with `grep -c`.

prompt: After the renames, the planner's imports still say `from '../planner.js'`, while the file is now `planner.ts`. What happens?

choices.text: The import breaks until every ending is changed to `.ts`
choices.why: The lesson says the opposite: the `.js` ending is not a mistake, and nothing has to change.

choices.text: Vite serves the old `planner.js`, left behind by the renames
choices.why: The loop moved the files, so no `planner.js` is left to serve.

choices.text: TypeScript reports TS2339 for the missing module
choices.why: TS2339 is a property that does not exist on a type; none of the 59 errors was about an import.

choices.text: It works: Vite finds `planner.ts` for it
choices.why: Right. From a TypeScript file, that is how imports of modules that will run as JavaScript are written.

prompt: `SessionRow` declares `session: Session` by type. What runtime check does Vue generate for that prop?
hint: What can Vue see of an interface while the app runs?

choices.text: A check of each field of `Session`, with a warning for a missing `minutes`
choices.why: The interface exists only for the checker; at run time there is nothing left to compare the fields against.

choices.text: `Object`, and that it is required
choices.why: Right. Vue can see that it received an object, and no more than that.

choices.text: None, since a type-based prop has no runtime half
choices.why: The compiler turns the type into the same runtime declaration lesson 6 wrote by hand.

choices.text: `String`, because `Session` is the name of a type
choices.why: The runtime type follows the shape of the value, an object, not the spelling of the type's name.

prompt: `addSession` takes `Omit<Session, 'id' | 'done'>`. What does that type give the planner? Choose all that apply.
hint: Read it as "a session without two fields".

choices.text: A caller that passes an id of its own is refused
choices.why: Right. The id is the rule's to fill in.

choices.text: A field added to `Session` later is required here at once
choices.why: Right. The type is derived from `Session`, so it follows every change to it.

choices.text: The new session's `done` starts as `false` because of it
choices.why: That is the function's body, `done: false`; a type puts no value anywhere.

choices.text: A session read from `courses.json` without `minutes` is caught when it loads
choices.why: Types are gone by the time the app runs; data that arrives over the network is not checked by them.

prompt: A new prop `label` must be optional, with the default `'Study'`. With `CourseCard`'s style, where do the two halves go?

choices.text: `label: string = 'Study'` inside the type passed to `defineProps`
choices.why: A type describes and holds no values; the default belongs to the destructuring.

choices.text: `{ type: String, default: 'Study' }` beside the type, in a second `defineProps`
choices.why: A component declares its props once; the object form and the type form are alternatives, not halves.

choices.text: `label?: string` in the type, `label = 'Study'` in the destructuring
choices.why: Right. That is how `planned?: number` and `planned = 0` are written, the Vue 3.5 form.

choices.text: `label: string` in the type, and `'Study'` set in `onMounted` if it is empty
choices.why: That leaves the prop required, so every parent that omits it is an error for the checker.

prompt: In `defineEmits<{ toggle: [id: string] }>()`, what is `[id: string]`?

choices.text: An array of ids the event collects
choices.why: The brackets are a type, not a value: no array is built.

choices.text: The listener's name, written as an array
choices.why: The listener is named by the parent, in `@toggle="..."`; this is what it receives.

choices.text: A runtime validator that rejects a number
choices.why: Vue keeps the event's name at run time, not a check of its arguments.

choices.text: A tuple: the event's arguments, one named string
choices.why: Right. An event with two would be `[id: string, done: boolean]`.

prompt: In the JavaScript planner, before any types, `SessionRow` called `emit('toggel', session.id)`. What would a student have seen?

choices.text: A warning in the console naming the unknown event
choices.why: The lesson says the console says nothing: an event with no listener is not an error.

choices.text: A box that does nothing when ticked, and no message
choices.why: Right. The event goes out and nobody is listening for that name.

choices.text: A blank page, because the component fails to compile
choices.why: Nothing about the event's name stops the component compiling; it renders as usual.

choices.text: The box ticks, since Vue corrects close spellings
choices.why: Vue matches event names exactly; `toggel` and `toggle` are two events.

prompt: A team declares `toggle: [id: string]` and a colleague, at run time, emits `toggle` with a number. What happens?
hint: Separate what the checker reads from what Vue keeps.

choices.text: Vue refuses the event at run time and logs the expected type
choices.why: That needs lesson 6's object form with a validator; the type keeps only the event's name.

choices.text: The event is dropped, because `toggle` is now treated as a native event
choices.why: The runtime list generated from the type is what tells Vue `toggle` is the component's own.

choices.text: If the code passed the checker, nothing stops it while it runs
choices.why: Right. The argument check is the half the type cannot keep at run time.

choices.text: The number is converted to a string on its way to the listener
choices.why: Neither Vue nor TypeScript converts anything; the listener receives the number.

prompt: What type does TypeScript give `ref([])` when nothing else is written?

choices.text: An array of `any`, which the checker lets through silently
choices.why: Under `strict`, a type that cannot be worked out is not a silent `any`; here it is an array of nothing.

choices.text: An array of `Session`, from the store's name
choices.why: TypeScript reads values, not names; `sessions` says nothing about its elements.

choices.text: A `Ref` holding `never[]`
choices.why: Right. Nothing can be read from a `never`, which is where the TS2339 errors came from.

choices.text: `null`, until the courses have loaded
choices.why: That is a template ref before mounting; an empty array is still an array.

prompt: In the store, `const courses = ref<___[]>([])` says what the array will hold.
hint: The interface `planner.ts` exports for a course.

prompt: `PlannerDialog` calls `dialog.value?.showModal()`. Why is the `?.` there?
hint: Lesson 9 showed when a template ref is filled.

choices.text: Because `showModal` does not exist on `HTMLDialogElement` in older browsers
choices.why: `<HTMLDialogElement>` is what makes `showModal` known to exist; the `?.` is about the ref.

choices.text: To silence TS7006 on the function's parameter
choices.why: These functions take no parameter; the error here was TS18047, `is possibly 'null'`.

choices.text: To make the dialog open faster
choices.why: `?.` changes nothing about speed; it only skips the call when the left side is empty.

choices.text: The ref is `null` until mount, and `?.` calls only if it is filled
choices.why: Right. The checker insists on the possibility, and `?.` handles it.

prompt: Once `routes` is typed `RouteRecordRaw[]`, `planner.hasCourse(to.params.id)` is refused. Why does the fix wrap it in `String(...)`?

choices.text: A parameter repeats in some URLs: `string | string[]`
choices.why: Right. `hasCourse` takes a `string`, and `String` makes one either way.

choices.text: Route parameters arrive as numbers, and course ids are strings
choices.why: Nothing in a URL arrives as a number; the type is `string | string[]`.

choices.text: `to` is still `any` and `String` gives it a type
choices.why: Typing `routes` is what gave `to` its type; that is why this second error appeared.

choices.text: `String` checks that the course exists before the guard runs
choices.why: `String` converts a value; the check is `hasCourse` itself.

prompt: Nothing in `TypedPicker` says what `item` is, yet `item.goal` is checked against `Course`. What decided that?

choices.text: The constraint `T extends { id: string }`
choices.why: The constraint says what any `T` must have; it does not pick which `T` this use is.

choices.text: `:items` was given a `Course[]`
choices.why: Right. The parent's use decides `T`, and the slot and the event follow.

choices.text: The `ref<Course | null>` declared for `chosen`
choices.why: `chosen` receives the event's value; it is not what fixes `T`.

choices.text: `TypedList` imports `Course` from the planner
choices.why: The list imports nothing about courses; that is the point of a generic.

prompt: In `TypedMistakes`, which of these does `vue-tsc` refuse? Choose all that apply.

choices.text: The `:key` on a session, because its `id` is `'s2'`
choices.why: `'s2'` is a string, which is all the constraint asks of `id`.

choices.text: `item.title` in the slot of the list of sessions
choices.why: Right. `T` became `{ id: string; minutes: number; }`, which has no `title`.

choices.text: `:items="labels"`, a list of strings
choices.why: Right. A string has no `id`, so `string[]` fails the constraint.

choices.text: Using `TypedList` twice in one template
choices.why: A component is used as many times as you like; each use decides its own `T`.

prompt: A parent passes `TypedList` the items `[{ id: 'g1', minutes: 20 }]` and its slot reads `item.minutes`. What does `vue-tsc` say?

choices.text: It refuses `item.minutes`, because the constraint names only `id`
choices.why: The constraint is a minimum; `T` is the whole shape that was passed, `minutes` included.

choices.text: It refuses the list, because a `Course` was expected
choices.why: `TypedList` knows nothing of courses; any shape with a string `id` is accepted.

choices.text: Nothing: it is accepted, and `minutes` is a number
choices.why: Right. `T` became `{ id: string; minutes: number; }`.

choices.text: It accepts it, but `item.minutes` is typed `any`
choices.why: A generic keeps the parent's types; losing them at the list's edge is what it exists to avoid.

prompt: The build script is now `vue-tsc --noEmit && vite build`. What does `&&` do there?

choices.text: Runs the two commands at the same time
choices.why: That is what `create-vue`'s helper package does; `&&` runs them one after the other.

choices.text: Runs `vite build` only if the checker succeeded
choices.why: Right. So a type error stops the build.

choices.text: Hands the checked files to `vite build`
choices.why: `--noEmit` writes nothing to hand over; Vite reads the sources itself.

choices.text: Runs `vite build` whatever the checker found, and reports both
choices.why: That would be `;`; with `&&` a failure ends the line.

prompt: Of the three places the lesson lists, which one tells you about a type error soonest?

choices.text: CI, on the pull request
choices.why: CI is the last of the three: it catches what nobody saw locally.

choices.text: `npm run type-check`, before a commit
choices.why: That is the middle one; it waits for you to run it.

choices.text: The dev server's terminal, as you save
choices.why: The dev server does not check types; the course does not add `vite-plugin-checker`.

choices.text: The editor, while you type
choices.why: Right. VS Code with *Vue (Official)* runs the same checker in the background and underlines the error.

prompt: A teammate's planner shows the week perfectly in the dev server, and `npm run type-check` reports four errors. What does that tell you?

choices.text: The errors are stale, since the dev server would have refused the files
choices.why: The dev server strips types and checks nothing, so it never refuses a file for a type error.

choices.text: Nothing contradicts: the code runs, and four places contradict its types
choices.why: Right. The planner ran all through this lesson while `vue-tsc` reported dozens.

choices.text: The errors are in files the page does not use
choices.why: The checker reads every file the `include` names; whether the page uses them is not what it reports.

choices.text: `vite build` will still succeed with the planner's build script
choices.why: Its build script runs the checker first, and `&&` stops on those four errors.

prompt: `du -sh node_modules/typescript` measured the compiler on disk. How many megabytes?
Why does a Vue project run `vue-tsc` rather than `tsc`, the plain TypeScript compiler?

choices.text: `tsc` is too slow for a project with components
choices.why: The difference the lesson names is about what each understands, not speed; TypeScript 7 is the faster one.

choices.text: `tsc` writes JavaScript files, and `vue-tsc` writes none
choices.why: Both accept `--noEmit`; what separates them is the file type they read.

choices.text: `tsc` does not understand `.vue` files, templates included
choices.why: Right. And `vue-tsc` has to be kept at a version that matches both Vue and TypeScript.

choices.text: `tsc` ignores `strict` from `@vue/tsconfig`
choices.why: `tsc` reads `extends` like any `tsconfig.json`; it simply cannot read a template.

prompt: By the lesson's reasoning, which of these is the weakest case for adding TypeScript from the start?
hint: The lesson weighs how long the code lives and how many people share its data.

choices.text: A booking app four people will change for years
choices.why: Long life and several people are the lesson's first reasons for types from the start.

choices.text: A dashboard whose order shape is shared by twenty components
choices.why: A data shape shared between many components is the planner's case, and a yes.

choices.text: A countdown widget on one page, written this afternoon
choices.why: Right. An afternoon's widget is fine in JavaScript, and converting it later is an afternoon's work.

choices.text: A shop whose libraries are Vue, Vue Router and Pinia
choices.why: Those libraries are written in TypeScript, so they cost nothing at their edges.

prompt: Put the steps of the planner's conversion in the order the lesson takes them.
hint: The checker can only find something once the files are TypeScript.
items: Rename the `.js` files and mark each `<script setup>`
Make the build run the checker first

prompt: Match each error code from this lesson to the cause it had in the planner.

pairs.right: A template ref that may be `null`
An event name that was not declared

prompt: Which of these exist only for the checker, with nothing of them left when the planner runs in the browser? Choose all that apply.
hint: Vue's compiler keeps a runtime half of some declarations.

choices.text: `interface Session` in `planner.ts`
choices.why: Right. Vite strips it, and the build's JavaScript is the same without it.

choices.text: The list of events from `defineEmits<{ toggle: [id: string] }>()`
choices.why: Vue generates a runtime list of declared events from it, which the fallthrough rule reads.

choices.text: `<HTMLDialogElement>` in `useTemplateRef<HTMLDialogElement>('dialog')`
choices.why: Right. The type argument only tells the checker which element it will be.

choices.text: `today?: boolean` in `SessionRow`'s props
choices.why: The compiler turns it into `{ type: Boolean, required: false }`, a runtime declaration.

choices.text: `Partial<Errors>` in `SessionForm`
choices.why: Right. It describes `shown` to the checker and produces no code.

prompt: A new `NoteRow` component declares `defineEmits<{ save: [text: string] }>()` and later calls `emit('save')` with no argument. Where is that found first, in this lesson's setup?

choices.text: In the browser's console, as a Vue warning when the event fires
choices.why: Vue keeps the event's name at run time, not its arguments, so nothing warns there.

choices.text: In the editor, underlined, by the checker comparing the call with the tuple
choices.why: Right. The tuple says one argument; the editor runs the same checker as you type.

choices.text: In the dev server's terminal, when the file is saved
choices.why: The dev server strips types and checks nothing.

choices.text: Nowhere: a missing argument is `undefined`, which a string accepts
choices.why: Under `strict`, `undefined` is not a `string`, and a missing argument is an error.
